status: drafted via lean single-pass workflow grounded in the real extracted verse text
notes: Galatians (Ethiopian) is Paul's tightest doctrinal letter - 6 short chapters, almost entirely argument/teaching rather than narrative, so the tier list leans heavily law/theme (8 of 12 tiers) around the book's real argumentative structure: the true-gospel warning (1:6-9), justification by faith vs. works of the law (2:15-21), Abraham's faith as the model (3:6-18), the law as a schoolmaster (3:19-29), the Hagar/Sarah two-covenants allegory (4:21-31), liberty vs. the flesh (5:1-15), the fruit of the Spirit vs. works of the flesh (5:16-26), and bearing one another's burdens (6:1-10) - all deliveredBy Paul, since he is the letter's sole voice throughout. Only 4 person tiers survive: Paul (author/apostle), Peter/Cephas (publicly withstood at Antioch, 2:11-14), James the Lord's brother (a "pillar," 1:19, 2:9), and Barnabas (Paul's companion to Jerusalem who is also, notably, personally swayed by the Antioch dissimulation in 2:13 - a real embodied action, not mere mention, so he earns his own tier rather than a submanager slot). Titus (present but uncircumcised, 2:1-3) is a submanager under Paul. John (grouped with James/Cephas as a "pillar" giving fellowship, 2:9) is a submanager under James, since the three are named together in that single verse and James is the one already given his own full tier here. NAMING-COLLISION FLAGS: this "James" is explicitly "the Lord's brother" (1:19), not James the son of Zebedee or James the son of Alphaeus - kept distinct per the naming-collision rule. This "John" is the apostle grouped with the Jerusalem pillars, not John the Baptist. Peter/Cephas is the same man under both names within this single letter (Paul himself uses both, e.g. "Cephas" in 2:9 and "Peter" in 2:11) - not a collision, a deliberate same-person dual-naming already explicit in the text, so kept as one character with both names noted. Abraham is referenced extensively (3:6-18) as the model of faith but never appears as an acting figure within Galatians itself - already fully indexed in Genesis, so he is logged in genealogyLists rather than re-indexed as a character, consistent with how OT genealogical references were handled for Matthew. No apocryphal/deuterocanonical content in this book - Galatians' canon and chapter/verse structure in this Ethiopian extraction matches the standard 6-chapter text exactly, no structural differences found versus KJV.

characters.name: Paul

verses.note: Identifies himself as an apostle, not sent by men but by Jesus Christ and God the Father.
Recounts his former life persecuting the church of God in the Jews' religion.
Describes being called by grace and going into Arabia and Damascus rather than to the apostles first.
After three years goes to Jerusalem to see Peter, abiding fifteen days.
Fourteen years later goes up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus by revelation.
Withstands Peter to the face at Antioch because he was to be blamed.
Notes he has written this large letter with his own hand.

funFacts: Paul's account of receiving the gospel directly "by the revelation of Jesus Christ" (1:12), without prior contact with the Jerusalem apostles, is the letter's central proof of his independent apostolic authority.

verses.note: Paul goes to Jerusalem specifically to see him, abiding with him fifteen days.
Called the one entrusted with the gospel of the circumcision, as Paul was with the uncircumcision.
Named alongside James and John as a "pillar," giving Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, here called Cephas.
Comes to Antioch and eats with the Gentiles, but withdraws and separates himself once certain men come from James, fearing the circumcision - publicly rebuked by Paul for it.
The only other apostle Paul saw on his first Jerusalem visit, explicitly identified as "the Lord's brother."
Named first among the three "pillars" (James, Cephas, John) who gave Paul and Barnabas fellowship.
Certain men "came from James" to Antioch, prompting Peter to withdraw from eating with the Gentiles.

characters.name: Barnabas

verses.note: Accompanies Paul on his second Jerusalem visit, fourteen years after the first.
Receives the right hand of fellowship alongside Paul from James, Cephas, and John.
Is personally "carried away" with the other Jews' dissimulation at Antioch, withdrawing from eating with the Gentiles alongside Peter.

funFacts: Barnabas is one of the few figures in Galatians shown being personally swayed by events rather than merely delivering doctrine, which is why he earns a full tier rather than a submanager slot under Paul.

verses.note: Taken by Paul to Jerusalem on the second visit.
Being a Greek, is not compelled to be circumcised - held up as proof against the false brethren's demands.

characters.name: John

verses.note: Named third of the three Jerusalem "pillars" (James, Cephas, John) who extend fellowship to Paul and Barnabas.

funFacts: Distinct from John the Baptist - this is John the apostle, named only once in Galatians, grouped with James and Cephas as a Jerusalem pillar.

characters.name: The True Gospel
characters.purpose: Warns that there is no "other" gospel - anyone, even an angel, preaching a different gospel than what was first preached is accursed (1:6-9).

verses.note: Paul marvels the Galatians are so soon removed to another gospel, and pronounces anyone preaching a different gospel accursed.

characters.name: Justification by Faith
characters.purpose: Teaches that no man is justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ (2:15-21).

verses.note: A man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ.
Paul declares he is crucified with Christ, yet lives by the faith of the Son of God.

characters.name: Abraham's Faith and the Promise
characters.purpose: Uses Abraham's faith, accounted to him for righteousness, to argue that those of faith - not those of the law - are Abraham's true children and heirs of the promise (3:6-18).

verses.note: Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.
The promises were made to Abraham and his seed - meaning one seed, which is Christ.

characters.name: The Law as Schoolmaster
characters.purpose: Explains the law's temporary role - added because of transgressions, serving as a schoolmaster to bring people to Christ until faith came (3:19-29).

verses.note: The law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ; after faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster.
There is neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female, for all are one in Christ Jesus.

characters.name: Two Covenants: Agar and Sarah
characters.purpose: Uses Abraham's two sons - one by the bondmaid Agar, one by the freewoman - as an allegory of the two covenants, bondage under the law versus freedom in the promise (4:21-31).

verses.note: The two covenants are identified: one from Mount Sinai, which gendereth to bondage - this is Agar.
Cites "cast out the bondwoman and her son" - concludes believers are children of the free, not the bondwoman.

characters.name: Liberty Wherewith Christ Made Free
characters.purpose: Calls believers to stand fast in the liberty Christ gave them, warning that seeking justification by circumcision/the law falls from grace (5:1-15).

verses.note: Stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
All the law is fulfilled in one word: thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.

characters.name: Fruit of the Spirit
characters.purpose: Contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit, calling believers to walk in the Spirit (5:16-26).

verses.note: Lists the works of the flesh - adultery, idolatry, hatred, and more - that exclude one from the kingdom of God.
Lists the fruit of the Spirit - love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance.

characters.name: Bear One Another's Burdens
characters.purpose: Closing exhortation on restoring the fallen in meekness, bearing one another's burdens, and doing good to all, especially the household of faith (6:1-10).

verses.note: Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
Let us not be weary in well doing, for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.

genealogyLists.note: Bulk/unresolved references kept out of the character list.

abraham_reference.note: Abraham is referenced extensively as the model of justification by faith and father of the promise, but never acts within Galatians itself - already fully indexed as a manager in the Genesis roster, not re-indexed here.
